newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sixty-two countries sign Brussels landmine ban.
newsitem.headline: Sixty-two countries sign Brussels landmine ban.

text.p: Sixty-two countries have so far signed the Declaration of Brussels preparing a landmine ban treaty and almost twice as many have promised to do so, Belgian diplomats said on Wednesday.

Informally 113 of the 115 countries taking part in the Brussels talks, which aim to prepare the signing of the first-ever treaty to ban the production, use, stockpiling and transfer of anti-personnel landmines, have pledged to sign the Brussels document, one diplomat said.
"This is only the second day (of the talks) and we are at 62. It is a good indication of the success we will have by the end," the diplomat said.
The treaty is due to be signed in Ottawa, Canada, in December 1997.
The signatories include African, Asian and central American countries as well as all 15 European Union nations with the exception of Greece and Finland.

Greece refuses to sign because of territorial disputes with Turkey while Finland refuses because of its long border with Russia. Russia and China, the main producers of landmines, are not taking part in the talks.

The U.S, which is attending with observer status, will not sign because it favours separate United Nations-sponsored landmine talks in Geneva. These talks, which require consensus, are not expected to produce a landmine ban for some years.

Diplomats said the U.S. delegation was actively trying to influence other countries not to sign the Brussels declaration, which has been made a precondition for participation in further rounds of the Ottawa landmine ban process, which was launched last year.
The Brussels conference is due to be followed by a conference in Oslo, Norway, in September where the exact wording of the landmine ban treaty will be negotiated ahead of the Ottawa signing.

Countries do not like the idea of being excluded from Oslo because they would not be able to influence the wording of the treaty. The U.S. does not believe the Brussels talks should be a precondition, diplomats said.
"(The U.S.) has tried to convince some people not to sign. I don't think they will succeed," one diplomat said. "Brussels is the only entry ticket to Oslo."

In addition to the U.S., 36 other delegations are taking part in the Brussels talks with observer status. They include Cuba, India, Indonesia, Iran, Israel, Libya, Pakistan, the Palestinian Authority and Turkey.
"This puts the U.S. in the company of a number of pariah states it wants to isolate on other fronts," an official of a non-governmental organisation attending the conference told Reuters.
